newsitem.title: JORDAN: Levy dismisses criticism of Jewish settlements.
newsitem.headline: Levy dismisses criticism of Jewish settlements.

text.p: Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy shrugged off on Thursday "exaggerated" international criticism of Jewish settlements on occupied Arab land and said his government would not bow to outside pressure.

Levy, speaking in Amman after meeting King Hussein and Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti, took a swipe at Kabariti and other leaders who condemned the settlements as a threat to peace after Israel offered financial benefits to West Bank settlers.

"The cry that has emanated regarding the question of settlements is purely an attempt to exaggerate this issue beyond its natural proportions," Levy, speaking through an interpreter, told a news conference in the grounds of the royal palace.
"Those who return to the question of settlements do so out of the intention to isolate Israel and pressure her to make concessions," he said. "That is not the method that will work."
U.S. President Bill Clinton, toughening his stance against the Israeli settlement revival, said this week the settlements were an obstacle to peace.
Jordan described Thursday's talks as "useful" and Levy said they were "productive".
But in a sign of public tension between the two neighbours, who signed a peace treaty two years ago ending a 46-year state of war, Kabariti stayed away from the press conference.
"The settlements are an illegal issue which contradict the principle of land for peace," he said earlier on Thursday. "And they are a direct threat to the overall peace process."
Some 140,000 Jews live in scattered settlements among over two million Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank.
When Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took office in June, pledging a tougher line on peace and promoting settlements, Jordan urged its dismayed Arab allies against pre-judging him.

But relations were strained by Netanyahu's decision in September to open a tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem, sparking widespread violence, and Jordan has spoken out increasingly against Israel's settlement policy.

Information Minister Marwan Muasher told the news conference there was a direct threat to Jordanian security as Israeli policy encouraged the idea that Palestinians could be pushed across the Jordan River to make way for Jews in the West Bank.

"In effect (it) will lead to the revival of the 'Jordan is Palestine' option," Muasher said. He said confidence in the ailing Middle East peace process could only revive if Israel implemented accords granting limited self-rule to Palestinians.
Levy in turn accused Arab states of exploiting the slow pace of talks between Israel and Palestinians to escalate friction.

"It is untenable that every time a difference of opinion or difficulty emerges...that these difficulties bring about a deterioration throughout the region and the creation of an atmosphere of distrust and hostility," he said.
Levy later inaugurated a new Israeli embassy building in Amman. Israeli diplomats have been operating from offices in a five-star hotel since they opened their mission to Jordan in December 1994.
